title: “LET THE ONE WITHOUT SIN CAST THE FIRST STONE”—BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN HOLDING A STONE ALL ALONG?
paragraphs: “LET THE ONE WITHOUT SIN CAST THE FIRST STONE”—BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN HOLDING A STONE ALL ALONG?

They dragged a guilty woman before Jesus, expecting Him to condemn her. But what happened next exposed the hearts of her accusers, revealed the holiness of God, and showed a kind of mercy that never makes peace with sin. This is the part of John 8:1–11 we cannot afford to misunderstand.
There is something terrifying about being exposed.
Not simply being caught doing something wrong.
Being exposed.
When the thing you prayed nobody would discover suddenly becomes the thing everybody is talking about.
When your worst decision becomes your reputation.
When people stop seeing your humanity and start seeing only your failure.
Imagine standing in front of a crowd that already knows your sin.
No opportunity to explain.
No one stepping forward to defend you.
Every face looking at you as though your entire life can be summarized by the worst thing you have ever done.
And then someone picks up a stone.
Now imagine something even more uncomfortable.
What if you are not the woman standing in the middle?
What if you are the person holding the stone?
Because the story of the woman caught in adultery is not merely about a sinner who needed mercy.
It is also about religious people who needed to discover how desperately they needed mercy themselves.
And before we finish this story, we need to confront one question:
Are we more interested in seeing sinners restored—or seeing them punished?
The answer may reveal more about our relationship with Jesus than we are prepared to admit.
The scene unfolds in John 8:1–11.
But before entering it, there is an important truth we must acknowledge if we want to handle Scripture faithfully.

The account commonly called the woman caught in adultery, traditionally located in John 7:53–8:11, is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John's Gospel. Other manuscripts preserve it, sometimes in different locations. For this reason, many modern Bible translations place the passage in brackets or include a textual note.

That does not mean we should pretend the account has no history or spiritual significance. It means we should be honest about its textual status. We cannot establish with certainty that John originally wrote these verses, and we should not build a doctrine upon this disputed passage alone.
Yet the mercy, holiness, repentance, and forgiveness reflected in this account can be examined alongside teachings firmly established throughout the New Testament.
And with that understanding, consider the scene the passage places before us.
Jesus is teaching in the temple.
People have gathered around Him.
Then suddenly, the atmosphere changes.
The scribes and Pharisees bring forward a woman caught in adultery.
They place her in the middle of the crowd.
Not quietly.
Not privately.
Publicly.
Her sin is now everybody's business.
Her shame has become a spectacle.
And her accusers have a question.
“Teacher, this woman was caught in adultery, in the very act.”
They appeal to the Law of Moses, then ask Jesus what He says should happen to her.
At first glance, it sounds like a question about righteousness.
But the passage exposes their actual intention.
They are testing Jesus, seeking grounds to accuse Him.
The woman is not their ultimate target.
Jesus is.
And suddenly the cruelty of the moment becomes even clearer.
A human being has been turned into a weapon in a religious confrontation.
Her humiliation is useful to them.
Her suffering is secondary.
Her future hardly seems to matter.
They want an answer that will trap Jesus.
And they are willing to destroy a woman in the process.
Does that sound painfully familiar?
Have you ever watched someone else's failure become entertainment?
A marriage collapses, and people rush to discuss the details.
A church leader falls into sin, and some people seem more excited about the scandal than grieved by the damage.
Someone confesses a struggle, and instead of receiving wise, truthful, compassionate help, they become the subject of whispered conversations.
A person's past resurfaces online, and strangers who know almost nothing about their life compete to deliver the harshest judgment.
Sometimes even Christians participate.
We call it defending righteousness.
We call it exposing darkness.
We call it standing for truth.
And sometimes exposing wrongdoing really is necessary, especially to protect victims, confront abuse, and pursue justice.
But there is a difference between confronting evil because we love what is right and enjoying another person's humiliation because it makes us feel superior.
You can speak the language of holiness while secretly feeding the appetite of pride.
That is what makes this account so disturbing.
The accusers know the Law.
But their hearts are being exposed by the very One they are attempting to trap.
There is another detail that should trouble us.
Where is the man?
The woman has been caught in adultery, yet only she is presented.

Under Leviticus 20:10 and Deuteronomy 22:22, the law concerning adultery addressed both parties. The precise legal circumstances matter, and the passage does not tell us everything that happened before this confrontation.
We cannot claim to know why the man is absent.
But his absence raises an unavoidable question about the consistency and motives of those bringing the accusation.
If this is truly about faithful obedience to God's Law, why is only one accused person standing there?
Selective outrage is not the same as biblical justice.
And religious hypocrisy becomes especially dangerous when it uses genuine moral truth as cover for dishonest motives.
Then Jesus does something nobody seems to expect.
He bends down.
And writes on the ground.
The Greek text uses the verb κατέγραφεν (kategraphen), describing His act of writing.
For centuries, readers have wondered what Jesus wrote.
The names of the accusers?
Their secret sins?
A passage from Scripture?
A warning?
Perhaps something connected to Jeremiah 17:13?
We do not know.
The passage never tells us.
And we should resist the temptation to turn an imaginative possibility into a biblical fact.
What matters is what Jesus actually says.
As the questioning continues, He straightens and declares:
“Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her.” — John 8:7, ESV
In Greek, the central expression is:
Ὁ ἀναμάρτητος ὑμῶν
Ho anamartētos hymōn.
“The one without sin among you.”
The word ἀναμάρτητος (anamartētos) means “without sin” or “sinless.”
But we need to be careful.
Jesus is not teaching that human courts must release every guilty person because judges and witnesses are sinners.
Nor is He teaching that Christians must never identify wrongdoing, confront sin, practice church discipline, or protect those who have been harmed.
That interpretation would contradict other clear biblical teachings, including Matthew 18:15–17, Galatians 6:1, and Romans 13:1–4.
The point is not that sin no longer matters.
The point is that these particular accusers cannot escape the examination of their own hearts.
They are attempting to use the Law against Jesus while their own motives are compromised.
And Jesus turns the moment of accusation into a moment of moral accountability.
Think about that.
They arrived expecting to examine a woman's guilt.
Instead, they found themselves standing before someone who could see through their performance of righteousness.
There are moments when Scripture does this to us.
We open the Bible looking for a verse that proves somebody else is wrong.
And suddenly, the Word confronts something we have been hiding.
Our bitterness.
Our dishonesty.
Our secret lust.
Our envy.
Our unforgiveness.
Our appetite for gossip.
Our habit of treating people as permanently disqualified because of failures we would desperately want forgiven if they were our own.
We are quick to recognize the sin that disgusts us.
Slower to recognize the pride that pleases us.
We condemn the person whose failure became public while protecting the sins that remain private.
And sometimes our greatest spiritual danger is not that we have stopped believing in God.
It is that we have become comfortable using God's truth without allowing it to transform our own hearts.
Jesus warned about this elsewhere.
In Matthew 7:3–5, He describes the absurdity of noticing a speck in another person's eye while ignoring a plank in our own.
Notice what He actually teaches.
Remove the plank first.
Then you can see clearly to help your brother.
He does not say the speck should remain forever.
He calls for repentance and clarity before correction.
That is the difference between self-righteous condemnation and humble restoration.
One wants to stand above another sinner.
The other remembers that every sinner needs grace.
And now the stones begin to fall.
Not because the woman has been declared morally innocent.
Not because adultery has become acceptable.
Not because God's holiness has changed.
But because the accusers begin leaving.
One by one.
The older ones first, according to the account.
We are not told exactly what each person thought or felt. We should not pretend to know their private reasons.
But the narrative makes the outcome unmistakable.
The public accusation collapses.
The crowd of accusers disappears.
And the woman remains before Jesus.
Imagine that moment.
The voices that had demanded her punishment are gone.
The people who treated her as an object lesson have walked away.
The woman who had been placed in the middle of a hostile crowd now stands before the One who has not joined their condemnation.
Then Jesus asks:
“Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you?”
She answers:
“No one, Lord.”
And Jesus says:
“Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.” — John 8:11, ESV
Do not rush past those words.
Because if we misunderstand them, we misunderstand the very heart of this story.
“Neither do I condemn you.”
And:
“Sin no more.”
Mercy.
And holiness.
Compassion.
And a call to change.
Not one without the other.
Jesus does not say, “Your adultery was never wrong.”
He does not say, “Continue living however you please.”
He does not announce that sin is an outdated concept invented by religious people.
He refuses to condemn her in this confrontation, and He calls her away from sin.
That distinction matters.
In the Greek text, the final instruction reads:
πορεύου, ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε
Poreuou, apo tou nyn mēketi hamartane.
“Go, and from now on sin no more.”
The command calls for a decisive departure from sinful living.
It is not a promise that she will never struggle again.
Nor does the passage tell us what happened afterward.
We are not given her name, her later testimony, or the story of her remaining years.
And that silence matters.
Because sometimes preachers tell this story as though Scripture describes her becoming a disciple, rebuilding her life, or following Jesus for decades.
Those may be moving possibilities.
But they are not recorded facts.
We must not add details simply because they make the ending more emotionally satisfying.
The words Jesus speaks are already powerful enough.
Mercy does not give sin permission to remain. Mercy opens the door to a life no longer ruled by it.
And here is where this story begins to reach beyond the temple courtyard.
Maybe you know what it feels like to be the woman.
Not necessarily because of adultery.
Maybe your marriage broke apart after decisions you deeply regret.
Maybe you betrayed someone's trust.
Maybe you fell into a pattern of sexual sin that left you feeling divided between the person you present publicly and the person you are privately.
Maybe you have spent years carrying the shame of addiction, dishonesty, bitterness, or a secret nobody knows.
Maybe you once served God with joy, but now you avoid prayer because you feel ashamed to approach Him.
You still believe in Jesus.
You still know the worship songs.
You still recognize the Bible verses.
But somewhere along the way, you began believing that your failure had become your identity.
And the hardest person to face is no longer the one who discovered your sin.
It is yourself.
You remember what you did.
You remember who was hurt.
You remember the opportunities you wasted.
You remember the promises you made to God and then broke.
And sometimes, even after you have confessed your sin, your memory continues acting like a courtroom.
The evidence is presented again.
The accusations return.
And you feel as though you must keep paying for something you cannot undo.
But hear this carefully.
The Christian Gospel does not teach that forgiveness makes consequences disappear.
Some relationships may need time to heal.
Some trust may never be fully restored.
Some actions require restitution, accountability, legal consequences, or long-term changes.
If you harmed someone, grace does not erase your responsibility toward them.
And if someone harmed you, forgiveness does not require you to deny what happened, abandon appropriate boundaries, or remain in danger.
Biblical mercy never requires us to pretend evil is harmless.
But neither does the Gospel teach that a repentant sinner must remain forever imprisoned beneath the identity of their worst failure.
Listen to the apostle Paul.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1, ESV
That is not a declaration that everybody is automatically forgiven regardless of their response to Christ.
It is a glorious promise concerning those who are in Him.
And Paul explains why.
God has acted through His Son to deal with sin.
The forgiveness Christians proclaim is not based on God pretending sin does not matter.
It is grounded in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
At the cross, the seriousness of sin and the depth of divine love meet.
Jesus, the sinless Savior, bears sin's judgment on behalf of His people.
He dies.
He is buried.
And He rises again.
That is the Gospel proclaimed in passages such as 1 Corinthians 15:3–4, Romans 3:23–26, and 1 Peter 2:24.
We must not flatten the distinction between the disputed account in John 8 and the full doctrine of salvation taught elsewhere in Scripture.
The passage itself does not narrate the cross or explain every dimension of justification.
But read in the light of the New Testament's wider testimony, it directs our attention toward a Savior whose mercy never requires Him to abandon righteousness.
And that changes everything.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that sin is imaginary.
It is the announcement that sin is so serious that we cannot save ourselves, and God's grace is so great that He sent His Son to save sinners.
The Greek word commonly translated “grace” is χάρις (charis).
It speaks of favor, gift, and gracious generosity.
In Ephesians 2:8–9, Paul teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not something earned by our works.
And verse 10 continues by describing believers as created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace is not purchased by our obedience.
Obedience is the fruit of a life being transformed by grace.
This is why the words “go, and sin no more” must never be separated from the mercy that precedes them.
Jesus does not offer forgiveness as a reward for becoming perfect first.
Nor does He call people to remain comfortable in rebellion.
He calls sinners to turn toward Him.
The biblical word for repentance, μετάνοια (metanoia), refers to repentance, a change of mind and direction involving a turning away from sin and toward God.
It is more than feeling embarrassed after getting caught.
More than crying because people found out.
More than promising to improve because consequences have become painful.
True repentance begins when we stop defending what God calls sin and turn toward the Savior who can forgive and change us.
Sometimes repentance is accompanied by tears.
Sometimes by confession.
Sometimes by the painful decision to end a relationship that dishonors God.
Sometimes by admitting that we need help with an addiction.
Sometimes by returning what we stole.
Sometimes by telling the truth after years of deception.
Sometimes by apologizing without demanding immediate forgiveness.
Sometimes by finally seeking accountability instead of making another private promise we have no plan to keep.
And sometimes repentance begins with a trembling prayer:
“Lord Jesus, I have been hiding. I have made excuses. I have called my sin a weakness when I knew I was choosing it. Please forgive me. Teach me to walk in Your truth.”
That is not weakness.
That is surrender.
But perhaps you have been reading this story and feeling strangely uncomfortable for a different reason.
You have not been imagining yourself as the accused woman.
You have been remembering the people you condemned.
The person whose failure you shared with others.
The friend whose confession became gossip.
The family member you quietly decided would never change.
The Christian who fell and whom you treated as though the grace of God had finally reached its limit.
Maybe you were technically correct about their wrongdoing.
But your attitude was wrong.
You wanted them exposed.
You wanted people to know.
You wanted the satisfaction of being proven right.
And deep down, their humiliation made you feel morally superior.
If that is you, the Gospel has something to say to you too.
You do not need to pretend your judgmental spirit was righteousness.
You can repent.
You can stop spreading the story.
You can apologize where appropriate.
You can make room for genuine restoration without minimizing harm or abandoning discernment.
Galatians 6:1 instructs those who are spiritual to restore someone caught in transgression in a spirit of gentleness, while watching themselves lest they also be tempted.
That is not moral indifference.
That is Christian maturity.
A mature believer does not celebrate sin.
But neither does a mature believer celebrate the destruction of a sinner.
And sometimes the person who most needs to hear “go, and sin no more” is not the one everybody is talking about.
It is the person who cannot stop talking about them.
There is a sentence worth carrying into every church conversation, every family conflict, and every social media controversy:
The truth of someone's sin never gives us permission to sin against them.
Let that settle.
Because it is possible to defend a biblical standard while violating biblical love.
It is possible to confront an actual wrong with an arrogant spirit.
It is possible to expose hypocrisy while being blind to our own.
And it is possible to become so fascinated with somebody else's scandal that we forget the reason Jesus came.
He came to save sinners.
Paul understood this personally.
In 1 Timothy 1:15, he calls himself the foremost of sinners while proclaiming that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.
This was a man who had persecuted the church.
He could not erase his past.
But his past was no longer the final authority over his identity.
The risen Christ had met him.
Grace had changed his direction.
And the man who once persecuted believers became a servant of the Gospel he had opposed.
That is why our theme at Gospel Warrior is more than a memorable phrase.
Not because every painful chapter disappears.
Not because the people we hurt automatically forget.
Not because repentance guarantees a trouble-free future.
But because Jesus can give a new direction to a life that seemed defined by sin, shame, and spiritual ruin.
He does not rewrite history by declaring evil good.
He changes people through truth, forgiveness, repentance, and His transforming grace.
Consider Peter.
He denied knowing Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
And after the resurrection, Jesus restored him and entrusted him with responsibility to care for His sheep, as recorded in John 21.
Consider the tax collector in Luke 18:9–14.
He did not approach God boasting about his righteousness.
He pleaded for mercy.
And Jesus said that he, rather than the self-righteous Pharisee, went home justified.
Consider the believers Paul addresses in 1 Corinthians 6:9–11.
After naming serious sins, Paul reminds them that some of them had once lived in those ways.
Then he speaks of their washing, sanctification, and justification in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
That is not the message of a Savior who merely tells guilty people to feel better.
It is the message of a Savior who truly saves.
And maybe that is what someone reading this needs to hear tonight.
You are not beyond the reach of Christ because your past is ugly.
You are not beyond His mercy because your struggle has lasted longer than you expected.
You are not disqualified from approaching Him because you are ashamed.
But you must not confuse His patience with permission to remain unchanged.
Come into the light.
Confess what you have been hiding.
Seek help where you need it.
Make things right where you can.
Trust the Savior who died and rose again.
And keep walking with Him.
First John 1:9 teaches that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
First John 2:1 also reminds believers that if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.
Those promises are not invitations to careless living.
They are reasons not to surrender to despair.
The enemy would love for you to believe there are only two possibilities.
Hide your sin.
Or be destroyed by your shame.
But the Gospel calls you to something better.
Bring your sin into the light of Christ.
Receive His forgiveness through faith.
And begin walking in repentance.
Not because you have become strong enough to rescue yourself.
But because the risen Jesus is a greater Savior than your sin is a master.
Not as a test of how religious you are.
Not as an invitation to reveal private details that belong in a safe conversation with a trusted pastor, counselor, or mature believer.
But as an opportunity for spiritual honesty.
Which person in this story do you recognize in yourself today?
The woman carrying shame?
The accuser holding a stone?
Or someone who knows that, in different seasons of life, you have been both?
You do not owe strangers your private story.
But you may discover that honest words of faith and repentance can encourage someone else who thought they were struggling alone.
And if this article brought someone to mind, please do not treat that thought as meaningless.
Perhaps you know a believer who has stopped attending church because shame has convinced them they are no longer welcome.
Perhaps you know someone who has become harsh, bitter, or quick to condemn.
Perhaps a friend has confused God's grace with permission to continue in sin.
Send it privately if that would be kinder.
And consider following Gospel Warrior and inviting your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who do not yet believe in Christ to follow along.
Not because following a page makes anyone more spiritual.
But because regular exposure to Scripture, faithful teaching, prayer, and Christian encouragement can help us keep our attention on the One who truly changes lives.
We want to do more than publish words that stir emotions for a moment.
We want to help people return to Scripture.
Understand the Gospel.
Recognize false ideas about God.
Grow in prayer.
Practice repentance.
Recover from spiritual discouragement.
And mature in their walk with Jesus Christ.
These resources are intended to help make biblical learning and spiritual nourishment more accessible.
And keeping a ministry of teaching, publishing, outreach, and resource development active requires real work, time, and financial support.
But I want to be clear about something important.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be reluctant or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
God is glorified through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, generosity, and sincere service—not through the size of a monthly payment.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Inviting a friend to read Scripture matters.
The Gospel is not for sale.
These products are not what makes the ministry valuable.
Jesus Christ is the reason the ministry exists.
The products are simply another way to carry encouraging messages into ordinary life, while supporting the continued work of Gospel Warrior.
Because the goal is not merely to build a larger audience.
It is to see more people know Jesus Christ, understand His Gospel, repent of sin, receive His grace, and grow into lives that reflect His truth and love.
Now return with me, one last time, to that temple courtyard.
The crowd has dispersed.
The accusers have gone.
The stones were not thrown.
And the woman has heard words that confront both her shame and her sin.
“Neither do I condemn you.”
“Go, and sin no more.”
Two truths that must remain together.
If we preach holiness without mercy, we may crush people beneath shame while forgetting our own desperate need for forgiveness.
If we preach mercy without repentance, we may comfort people in the very sin from which Christ calls them to turn.
But the Gospel of Jesus Christ gives us neither cruelty disguised as righteousness nor permissiveness disguised as love.
It gives us the crucified and risen Savior.
The One who calls us to repent.
The One who receives sinners who come to Him.
The One who forgives.
The One who transforms.
The One who teaches His people to speak truth without abandoning love.
And perhaps the most searching question is not whether you have ever committed a sin worthy of public shame.
Romans 3:23 already tells us that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
The question is what you will do when the truth of your own sin confronts you.
Will you hide?
Will you excuse it?
Will you point to someone worse?
Will you keep holding a stone so nobody notices the condition of your own heart?
Or will you come to Jesus?
You can put down the stone.
You can stop pretending.
You can confess what is wrong.
You can seek forgiveness and begin making things right.
You can turn from the sin that has been destroying you.
And you can trust the Savior who did not remain in the grave.
Do not mistake the silence of the accusers for the end of the story.
The deepest question is what happens when a sinner encounters the truth and mercy of Jesus Christ.
Because the goal of grace is not simply to leave you feeling less ashamed.
It is to lead you into a restored relationship with God and a transformed life.
So before you leave this article, remember this:
The hands that once held stones can be opened in repentance, and the heart that once hid in shame can be brought into the light of Christ.
And if you remember only one thing, let it be this:
Your sin must never be defended, your wounds must never be dismissed, and your story does not have to end where your shame began—because Jesus Christ is still mighty to save.
